use: Use video when learners benefit from hearing an explanation, seeing a demonstration, or observing expert reasoning.
d: Give each video one clear purpose and aim for approximately 5–10 minutes.
Use a conversational script focused on what learners should notice, understand, or do next.
Plan narration and visuals together, and consider adding an in-video question at a purposeful pause.
a: Review and correct auto-generated captions, especially names and specialized terminology.
Describe meaningful visual information aloud.
Do not rely on color, visual position, sound, or animation alone to communicate meaning.
c: Use original, licensed, public-domain, or appropriately permissioned media.
Obtain permission from guests and anyone else featured in the recording.
Confirm that permissions cover distribution through a public, global Course.

use: Use a Reading when learners need a detailed explanation, reference, worked process, or resource they can review at their own pace.
d: Begin with what learners should gain from the Reading and how they will use it.
Use informative headings, short sections, concise paragraphs, and descriptive links.
Separate essential content from optional detail, and use graphics, tables, or code when they support the learner’s task.
a: Use a logical heading structure and alternative text for meaningful images.
Identify table headers clearly and describe complex charts or diagrams.
Make code, charts, and linked or embedded content accessible.
c: Confirm permission before reproducing articles, chapters, figures, tables, code, or substantial excerpts.
Link to lawful external sources when learners do not need the content reproduced in Coursera.
Attribute third-party materials as required.

use: Use an Interactive Plugin when learners need to manipulate information, explore a model, use an external tool, or see how their choices affect an outcome.
d: Give learners a specific task or question rather than asking them simply to “explore.”
Explain how to begin, what to manipulate or observe, and what they should conclude or produce.
Include follow-up questions or feedback that help learners interpret the experience.
a: Confirm that essential controls and information can be accessed without relying solely on dragging, hovering, color, or precise pointer movement.
Identify device, browser, account, and technical requirements in advance.
Provide an alternative path if the plugin is inaccessible or unavailable.
c: Confirm that the tool and its content may be embedded or linked within Coursera.
Review licenses and permissions for included media, data, simulations, and other content.
Consult the project team about accounts, data collection, privacy, or other conditions associated with the tool.

use: Use Coach Dialogue for a personalized, AI-supported conversation that helps learners explain their reasoning, reflect, make decisions, or apply Course concepts.
d: Define what learners should accomplish through the conversation.
Give the AI coach a clear role, source material, response criteria, and boundaries.
Prompt learners to explain their thinking and end with a reflection or other output.
a: Provide clear instructions and make key concepts and criteria available outside the conversation.
Do not require learners to disclose personal, medical, employment, or other sensitive information.
Provide another way to engage with the objective if the conversational format creates a barrier.
c: Use original or appropriately permissioned scenarios, prompts, frameworks, and reference material.
Do not ask learners to enter copyrighted, confidential, personally identifiable, or employer-owned content.
Attribute frameworks and other sources incorporated into the Coach Dialogue.

use: Use Coach Role Play when learners need to practice an interpersonal or job-related skill through a realistic conversation with an AI persona.
d: Define the situation, learner role, AI persona, goal, and relevant context.
Identify the behaviors or communication strategies learners should practice.
Align feedback with Course criteria and, when possible, let learners reflect, retry, and apply the feedback.
a: Clearly explain the scenario, roles, expectations, and how to exit or restart.
Do not make the experience depend on speech, audio, speed, or a particular communication style unless essential.
Review personas and situations for cultural assumptions, stereotypes, sensitive content, and unnecessary disclosure.
c: Create original or appropriately permissioned personas, scenarios, rubrics, and supporting materials.
Do not recreate real people, copyrighted characters, proprietary cases, or confidential workplace situations without authorization.
Confirm permission before adapting published cases, scripts, or professional exercises.

use: Use Assessments to provide practice and feedback or to determine whether learners have achieved a Module objective.
note: Each Module must include at least one graded assessment. Ungraded assessments can provide checkpoints and practice before graded work.
d: Begin with the objective and identify what learners must do to demonstrate it.
Assess the intended learning rather than unnecessary complexity, trivia, or recall alone.
Provide plausible answer choices, explanatory feedback, and practice with a similar skill before graded work.
a: Make question text, response options, feedback, rubrics, images, graphs, and code accessible.
Use concise, direct language and avoid unnecessary time pressure.
Do not rely on color, sound, visual position, or an image alone to communicate information.
c: Write original questions or confirm permission to use licensed question banks.
Clear cases, datasets, images, code, quotations, and other third-party materials.
Do not require learners to upload copyrighted, proprietary, or confidential materials.

use: Use Programming Assignments when learners need to write, modify, debug, or evaluate code.
d: Clearly describe the task, expected inputs and outputs, constraints, and evaluation criteria.
Provide starter code, examples, documentation, and test cases appropriate to the learner’s experience.
Break complex assignments into stages and provide feedback that helps learners diagnose and correct errors.
a: Provide instructions, code, error messages, and feedback as selectable text.
Use consistent formatting and explain specialized syntax, filenames, and directory structures.
Do not use color alone to distinguish errors, changes, or code states.
c: Check licenses for starter code, datasets, libraries, packages, and APIs.
Preserve required open-source notices and attribution.
Do not include proprietary code, credentials, private repositories, or confidential data.

use: Use Coursera Labs when learners need a configured, in-browser environment to practice with code, data, software, or other technical tools.
d: State the task, expected outcome, approximate time, prior knowledge, and technology requirements before learners begin.
Minimize setup and include only the tools, packages, and files learners need.
Break the work into stages and explain how learners can test progress, recover from errors, restart, and confirm completion.
a: Review the accessibility of the complete environment, including editors, consoles, visualizations, and embedded tools.
Ensure instructions and essential controls can be accessed with a keyboard and assistive technology.
Provide an alternative when the environment creates a barrier unrelated to the learning objective.
c: Confirm that software, packages, datasets, templates, and starter files may be installed or distributed in the Lab environment.
Follow applicable open-source and commercial license requirements.
Remove proprietary information, credentials, and sensitive or personally identifiable data.
